title: Affirming the consequent
claim: Every even integer is divisible by 4.
proof_steps: If an integer is divisible by 4, then it is even.
Let n be even.
Therefore n is divisible by 4.
counterexample: n=6 is even but not divisible by 4.
notes: The proof reverses a one-way implication.

title: One-sided biconditional
claim: For integers n, n is divisible by 6 iff n is divisible by 2.
proof_steps: Assume n is divisible by 6.
Then n=6k=2(3k), so n is divisible by 2.
Therefore the biconditional holds.
counterexample: n=2 shows the omitted converse is false.
notes: Only the forward direction was proved, and the converse is false.

title: Even square
claim: The square of an even integer is even.
proof_steps: Let n be even, so n=2k for some integer k.
Because 2k^2 is an integer, n^2 is even.
notes: Direct witness proof.

title: Hidden division by zero
claim: If a=b then 2=1.
proof_steps: Assume a=b.
Then a^2=ab.
Subtract b^2 to get (a-b)(a+b)=b(a-b).
Cancel a-b to get a+b=b.
Using a=b gives 2b=b, hence 2=1.
missing_assumption: a-b must be nonzero to cancel it, but the hypothesis gives a-b=0.
counterexample: a=b=1 satisfies the hypothesis while 2 is not 1.
notes: The first invalid operation is cancellation by zero.

lean.scope_note: Checks the failing cancellation step at a = b = 1 rather than the absurd conclusion.

title: Positive derivative
claim: If f'(x)>0 on an interval, then f(x)>0 there.
proof_steps: Assume f'(x)>0 throughout I.
Therefore f is strictly increasing on I.
Therefore f(x)>0 on I.
counterexample: f(x)=x on I=(-2,-1) has f'=1>0 but f<0.
notes: Monotonicity does not determine vertical position.

lean.scope_note: Refutes the claim on the interval (-2, -1).

title: Continuous maximum on compact set
claim: A continuous real-valued function on [0,1] attains a maximum.
proof_steps: The interval [0,1] is compact.
The continuous image f([0,1]) is compact in R.
A nonempty compact subset of R contains its supremum, so f attains a maximum.
notes: The interval is nonempty, and the extreme-value argument is valid.

title: Open interval maximum
claim: Every continuous function on (0,1) attains a maximum.
proof_steps: Let f be continuous on (0,1).
The domain is bounded.
Therefore the extreme value theorem implies f attains a maximum.
missing_assumption: The domain should be compact, for example [0,1], rather than merely bounded.
counterexample: f(x)=x on (0,1) is continuous and bounded but has no maximum.
notes: Boundedness does not replace compactness in the extreme value theorem.

title: Integral and pointwise limit
claim: Pointwise convergence permits exchanging limit and integral.
proof_steps: Let f_n converge pointwise to f on [0,1].
Integrate both sides of the pointwise limit.
Conclude lim_n integral f_n = integral f.
missing_assumption: A condition such as dominated convergence, uniform convergence, or another applicable interchange theorem is needed.
counterexample: f_n(x)=n on (0,1/n) and 0 otherwise converges pointwise a.e. to 0, but each integral equals 1.
notes: The stated hypotheses do not justify the interchange.

lean.scope_note: Machine-checks the counterexample sequence (n+1)·1_(0,1/(n+1)); the INCOMPLETE verdict itself is informal.

title: Symmetric implies PSD
claim: Every real symmetric matrix is PSD.
proof_steps: A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues.
Therefore all its eigenvalues are nonnegative.
Hence x^T A x is nonnegative for all x.
missing_assumption: Assume A is PSD, equivalently all eigenvalues are nonnegative.
counterexample: A=[-1] is symmetric and has a negative eigenvalue.
notes: Reality of eigenvalues does not imply their nonnegativity.

title: PSD square root
claim: Every real symmetric PSD matrix has a real symmetric PSD square root.
proof_steps: By the spectral theorem, A=Q Lambda Q^T with Q orthogonal and Lambda diagonal.
PSD implies every diagonal entry lambda_i is nonnegative.
Set B=Q diag(sqrt(lambda_i)) Q^T.
Then B is symmetric PSD and B^2=A.
notes: Standard spectral construction.

lean.scope_note: Mathlib's PosSemidef over ℝ includes symmetry.

title: PSD implies invertible
claim: Every PSD matrix is invertible.
proof_steps: For all x, x^T A x is nonnegative.
Therefore x^T A x is positive for every nonzero x.
Hence the null space is trivial and A is invertible.
missing_assumption: Positive definiteness, not semidefiniteness, is sufficient here.
counterexample: The zero matrix is PSD and singular.
notes: Nonnegative was silently strengthened to strictly positive.

title: Stationary point is global minimum
claim: Every differentiable stationary point is a global minimum.
proof_steps: Let x* satisfy grad f(x*)=0.
Therefore x* is a local minimum.
Every local minimum is global, so x* is global.
missing_assumption: Convexity would make stationarity sufficient for global optimality under standard differentiability assumptions.
counterexample: f(x)=-x^2 has grad f(0)=0, but 0 is a strict local maximum.
notes: Stationarity alone does not even imply local minimality.

title: Strongly convex stationary point
claim: A stationary point of a differentiable strongly convex function is its unique global minimizer.
proof_steps: Strong convexity gives f(y) >= f(x*) + grad f(x*)^T(y-x*) + (mu/2)||y-x*||^2 for mu>0.
At a stationary point grad f(x*)=0.
Thus f(y) >= f(x*) + (mu/2)||y-x*||^2, with strict inequality for y not equal to x*.
Therefore x* is the unique global minimizer.
notes: The conclusion follows directly from strong convexity.

lean.scope_note: One real variable only, under strict (weaker than strong) convexity; ℝⁿ is not covered.

title: Uncorrelated implies independent
claim: Uncorrelated random variables are independent.
proof_steps: Assume Cov(X,Y)=0.
Then E[XY]=E[X]E[Y].
Therefore the joint distribution factors, so X and Y are independent.
missing_assumption: Joint Gaussianity is one common sufficient additional assumption.
counterexample: Let X be uniform on {-1,0,1} and Y=X^2. Then Cov(X,Y)=0, but Y is determined by X.
notes: One moment identity does not imply factorization of the joint law.

title: Linearity of expectation
claim: Expectation is linear without an independence assumption.
proof_steps: Let X and Y be integrable random variables.
By linearity of the integral, E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y].
No independence assumption is required.
notes: Integrability is enough for this finite linearity statement.

lean.scope_note: Integrability of each summand is assumed, as it must be.

title: Expectation through square
claim: For every square-integrable X, E[X^2]=(E[X])^2.
proof_steps: The function t^2 is continuous.
Therefore expectation commutes with squaring.
Hence E[X^2]=(E[X])^2.
missing_assumption: Equality holds when X is almost surely constant; generally Jensen gives an inequality.
counterexample: For X in {-1,1} with equal probability, E[X]=0 while E[X^2]=1.
notes: Continuity does not license moving a nonlinear function through expectation.

title: Asymptotic equivalence as equality
claim: sin x equals x for all sufficiently small nonzero x.
proof_steps: We know sin x ~ x as x approaches 0.
Therefore sin x=x in a neighborhood of 0.
counterexample: For every sufficiently small positive x, sin x < x.
notes: Asymptotic equivalence is a limiting ratio, not eventual equality.

title: Minimum of nonempty bounded set
claim: Every nonempty bounded subset of R has a minimum.
proof_steps: Let S be nonempty and bounded below.
By completeness, inf S exists.
Therefore inf S belongs to S and is its minimum.
missing_assumption: Closedness is a natural sufficient addition for a nonempty set bounded below in R.
counterexample: S=(0,1) is nonempty and bounded below, but has no minimum.
notes: An infimum need not be attained.

title: Handshake lemma
claim: The sum of degrees in a finite undirected graph equals twice the number of edges.
proof_steps: Count vertex-edge incidences by summing degrees over vertices.
Every undirected edge contributes exactly two incidences, one at each endpoint, with a loop counted twice under the standard degree convention.
Therefore sum_v deg(v)=2|E|.
notes: Valid double-counting proof for finite undirected graphs.

lean.scope_note: Simple graphs only; multigraphs and loops are not covered.

title: Continuous image of compact set
claim: The continuous image of a compact space is compact.
proof_steps: Let U be an open cover of f(K).
The preimages f^{-1}(U) form an open cover of K.
Compactness of K gives a finite preimage subcover.
The corresponding original open sets form a finite cover of f(K).
notes: Standard open-cover proof; continuity licenses openness of preimages.
